blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Sliced inference such as SAHI is the standard remedy for small objects in high-resolution imagery, but its gains are usually measured against low-resolution baselines. We revisit sliced inference with scale as the explicit variable and ask when tiling actually pays off. We compare seven dense detectors from four families on VisDrone and DOTA, under pre-specified hypotheses, calibration-only tuning and a single evaluation on held-out test data. Two findings emerge. First, much of the benefit attributed to slicing is a resolution effect: on VisDrone, a single pass trained at a higher resolution outperforms tiling with box fusion (merging decoded boxes) for every detector that could be trained at that resolution, and at equal compute a higher resolution helps more than a larger model. Second, tiles carry complementary information that box fusion wastes. We introduce SCAHI (Slicing with Coverage-Aware Hyper Inference), which accumulates the dense outputs of all passes with weights that give every image position the same total coverage, and reads objects off a peak grid fine enough to keep crowded neighbours apart. On identical passes, SCAHI outperforms box fusion for every YOLO detector on both datasets and matches it for FCOS. On DOTA, whose images far exceed the resolution a single pass can be trained at, tiles with SCAHI beat the best single pass for every detector, by 4.3 to 5.6 mAP50 at 2048 px, and replacing only SAHI's merge step by SCAHI adds 2.3 to 4.0 mAP50. An ablation attributes the gain to the border weighting and the resolution of the peak grid. Source code is available at https://github.com/beckerio/scahi.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Tiling a large image into overlapping slices and running the detector on each slice is routine for small objects in drone
and satellite imagery [ 2 ] . The reported gains are large, but they are usually measured against a full-image
baseline at a low input resolution. This mixes two effects. A tile shows a part of the image at a larger scale, which helps
small objects, but the same effect can be obtained by feeding the whole image at a higher resolution. On
VisDrone [ 25 ] , a typical image has a long side of about 1360 px, and a 640 px tile at native scale shows
objects at almost the same size as a full image resized to 1280 px.

blocks.en:
We therefore treat scale as the explicit variable and compare every sliced configuration with a single pass trained and
run at a matched or higher resolution. All comparisons use one evaluation code path per dataset, a calibration split for
every tunable choice, hypotheses fixed before the corresponding results existed, and a single evaluation on held-out test
data. We use two datasets that represent two regimes. On VisDrone, images are moderately large, and a single pass at the
native resolution can be trained. On DOTA [ 23 ] , images are several thousand pixels wide and densely populated,
and training a single pass beyond 2048 px exceeds the memory of our GPU.

blocks.en: 2 Related work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Sliced inference. SAHI [ 2 , 1 ] popularised slicing-aided inference and
fine-tuning. Follow-ups make slicing cheaper or adaptive: ASAHI [ 11 ] fixes the number of slices,
DAHI [ 19 ] and GOIS [ 12 ] select dense regions, ROI-Gated
SAHI [ 14 ] selectively applies sliced inference to regions identified by a lightweight object proposer,
skipping background regions when foreground coverage is low, and ESOD [ 10 ] slices at feature level. Earlier, ClusDet [ 24 ] and DMNet [ 7 ] chose crops from cluster or density
maps. These works compare against full-image baselines at a fixed, usually low, input size; matched-resolution baselines
are rarely reported.

blocks.en:
Merging detections. Multi-pass inference needs a merge step: NMS, Soft-NMS [ 3 ] , SAHI’s greedy
non-maximum merging [ 2 ] , or Weighted Boxes Fusion [ 18 ] . All operate on decoded boxes.
Voting-based detectors such as HoughNet [ 15 ] accumulate evidence for objects within a single pass;
SCAHI instead merges the outputs of overlapping passes with coverage-aware weights. Weighted aggregation of overlapping
windows is standard in semantic segmentation, for example Gaussian-weighted sliding
windows in nnU-Net [ 5 ] . There, the aggregated map is the output. In detection, individual objects must
afterwards be separated from the aggregated evidence, and, as we show, this step decides whether multi-pass inference pays off.

blocks.zh: 3 研究设计

blocks.en:
Datasets and metrics. On VisDrone2019-DET [ 25 ] we use the standard 10 classes and the toolkit
AP@[.5:.95] with ignore regions treated as in the official toolkit, whose evaluation we ported and validated against the
original. On DOTA v1.5 [ 4 ] we use horizontal boxes, all 16 classes and the official mAP50 of the DOTA devkit,
again through a validated port, without a cap on detections per image. The devkit ignores objects marked difficult ,
which include all objects below 8 px; a pre-specified secondary evaluation counts them as normal objects. To bound memory,
the DOTA pipeline keeps at most 200,000 detections per image (for box fusion, per pass); on VisDrone, every method is capped at
500 detections per image, as in the toolkit. We call an object crowded if another object of the same class overlaps it
with IoU > 0.3 >0.3 , and isolated otherwise; the recall of both groups is measured at IoU 0.5.

For every detector that could be trained at 2048 px (all but YOLOv12m), the single pass beats the 1280 px pass with tiles

confirmed across detectors on both splits. Whether tiles with SCAHI also beat the 2048 px single pass (Q3) depended on the

and YOLOv12m could not be tested, so Q3 is not confirmed on val. On test-dev, all four testable detectors exceed the threshold;
as verdicts are taken on val, this counts as supporting evidence only.

blocks.en:
Decomposition and over-merging (post hoc). Splitting the step from the single pass to tiles with SCAHI shows that
the tiles add a similar amount for every detector, 1.1–1.5 AP at 2048 px on test-dev, almost entirely on objects below
16 px ( Fig. 4 ). The difference lies in fusing the single pass itself: it helps detectors with NMS but costs
YOLOv10, whose one-to-one head already separates crowded objects. With a cell factor of 5, the fused single pass loses 22 to
24 points of recall on objects with a same-class neighbour. The refined grid recovers most of it and adds 1.2–1.4 AP on val
for every detector; on test-dev the gain is about half as large (0.6–0.8 AP) but positive for every detector, the expected
shrinkage after a search. With it, tiles beat the 2048 px single pass on test-dev by 1.0–3.3 AP for every detector.

DOTA represents the other regime ( Tab. 3 ). Its images are several thousand pixels wide and contain up to ten thousand
objects. Because of this density, training a single pass at 3072 px exceeded the memory of our GPU even with a batch of two,
and YOLOv12s could not be trained beyond 1024 px. Here tiles pay off. Because the refined grid was fixed before any DOTA result existed, DOTA tests it on independent data.
Tiles at native resolution with SCAHI beat the strongest
trainable single pass for all five detectors: by 4.3 to 5.6 mAP50 at 2048 px, and by 9.6 for YOLOv12s on its weaker 1024 px
pass (Q3). Counting the difficult objects, the gains grow (e.g. 6.3 and 5.0 for YOLOv10s/m), and AP@[.5:.95] shows the same
picture (supplement). For the YOLO detectors, SCAHI beats box fusion on identical passes at every testable resolution (Q2); for FCOS, both fusions
perform on par ( + 0.4 +0.4 and + 0.1 +0.1 mAP50, not confirmed). Q1 holds for YOLOv10m and YOLOv11s but narrowly misses for YOLOv10s

blocks.en:
Two analyses on VisDrone clarify what limits small objects. Recall as a function of object size in the network input is
the same whatever the inference resolution, so tiles and a higher input resolution help in the same way; below
about 6 input pixels almost nothing is found. A degradation test suggests that the remaining difficulty of small objects stems
more from the objects themselves, often occluded and crowded, than from missing pixels: large objects that lose half their
resolution lose only 0.03 in recall, while originally small objects at the same apparent size are 0.09 below them. Training
only on objects within a valid size band per zoom level, in the spirit of SNIPER, brought no gain over ignore-aware training.

blocks.en: 6 Discussion and limitations
blocks.zh: 6. 讨论和限制

blocks.en:
When does sliced inference pay off? We observed two regimes. Where the image could be processed at the needed
resolution in a single pass, as on VisDrone, a higher input resolution was the cheaper route and outperformed standard tiling
for every detector. Where the resolution a single pass could be trained at fell short of the image, as on DOTA, tiles paid off
clearly. Which regime applies depends on image size, object density and the available memory, so the boundary will shift
with hardware and detector. For the YOLO detectors, a dense fusion that keeps neighbours apart turned the tiles into more
accuracy than box fusion in both regimes; for FCOS, both fusions were on par, and the reason, a peak grid too coarse for
crowded scenes, is the same mechanism that the refined grid addresses. Per image, the gain of tiles with SCAHI increased with the share of small objects on DOTA (Spearman ρ = 0.15 \rho=0.15 to 0.21 0.21 ); on VisDrone this relation was weak ( | ρ | ≤ 0.09 |\rho|\leq 0.09 ), and in neither dataset did it follow the
share of crowded objects (supplement). Like any tiled inference, including SAHI, SCAHI multiplies the number of passes; most of
its cost comes from these passes, and the fusion adds the remainder. It therefore targets accuracy-oriented processing of large
images, such as offline analysis of aerial imagery; where latency matters more than the last points of accuracy, a single pass
at the highest trainable resolution remains the better choice.

Limitations. (i) SCAHI requires dense per-position predictions, as
produced by anchor-free heads (YOLO, FCOS [ 21 ] , GFL [ 8 ] ); query-based detectors such as RT-DETR output a fixed set of predictions per
pass and would require a sparse variant of the fusion, which we leave for future work. Apart from FCOS on DOTA, our experiments use YOLO detectors. (ii) On VisDrone, the refined peak grid was found post
hoc; its held-out gain is about half of its val estimate, and on DOTA it was pre-specified. Its cell factor is selected by
mAP50 on a calibration split, which can miss crowded scenes when they are rare, as for FCOS; a selection criterion that
accounts for crowded recall is left for future work. (iii) The DOTA devkit ignores the
smallest objects, and the images we used are re-encoded JPEGs. (iv) All latencies were measured on a single RTX 5090, each table in one exclusive run. (v) Horizontal boxes only.

blocks.en: 7 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 7 结论

blocks.en:
In our experiments, whether sliced inference pays off depended on whether the needed resolution could be trained.
On VisDrone, where it could, a single pass at a higher resolution beat tiling with box fusion;
on DOTA, where it could not, tiles added substantial accuracy for every detector. For the YOLO detectors, the merge step
decided in both regimes: a dense fusion with coverage-aware weights and a peak grid that keeps neighbours apart turns the
information in the tiles into accuracy that box fusion leaves on the table.

在VisDrone上,在它可以做到的地方,一个高分辨率的单次传球用盒式聚变击败了板块;
在DOTA上,如果它不能,瓦片为每个探测器增加了相当的精度. 对于YOLO探测器,合并步骤
在两种体制中决定的:密集的聚变,具有覆盖感的重量,以及使邻居分开的高峰网格

blocks.en:
Frozen evaluation. Before each test-dev evaluation, all configurations to be evaluated were frozen together with the
checksums of their weights and the origin of every choice (fixed by design or selected on calib). A replay through the test-dev
code path then had to reproduce the val result of every frozen configuration exactly before test-dev was touched. Test-dev was evaluated once per study, and every frozen
configuration is reported.

报告配置情况。

blocks.en:
Environment and compute. Python 3.11, PyTorch 2.14.1 (CUDA 13.0), Ultralytics 8.4.183, SAHI 0.12.8. All runs used one
NVIDIA RTX 5090 (32 GB) at the default power limit; the study moved once between two identical machines, and the frozen
weights reproduced every val result exactly on both. All latencies were measured on one machine with exclusive use of the GPU, each table in one run. Parts of the calibration tuning were
parallelised; a cross-check confirmed identical selections and identical results. The main study
took about 24 GPU-hours plus CPU time for the fusion.

blocks.en: 11 DOTA: protocol and detailed results
blocks.zh: 11 DOTA:协议和详细结果

blocks.en:
Data. We use DOTA v1.5 with the official horizontal-box annotations; the official boxes coincide with the minimum and
maximum of the oriented corners for every object. Train and val contain 280,196 instances. The images used are JPEG files
re-encoded at quality 70, which we report as a limitation. One training image (P1872) whose annotations lie far outside the
image was excluded from training and calibration. All objects below 8 px and about three quarters of those between 8 and
16 px are marked difficult ; they are used as normal positives in training, ignored by the official evaluation, and
counted in the pre-specified secondary evaluation “all objects”.
blocks.zh:
数据。 我们使用DOTA v1.5, 带有官方水平框说明; 官方框与最小和
每个对象的最大方向角。 火车和Val载有280,196个实例。 使用的图像为 JPEG 文件
重新编码在质量70, 我们报告作为一个限制。 一个培训形象(P1872),其说明远远超出
图像被排除在培训和校准之外。 8px以下的所有物体,以及8和8之间约四分之三的物体。
16 px是标记困难的;它们被用作训练中的正常阳性,被官方评价忽略,和
列入预先指定的次级评价的“所有目标”。

blocks.en:
Evaluation. Our port of the official DOTA devkit evaluation (horizontal boxes) reproduces the original exactly on
synthetic and realistic detections. The primary metric has no cap on detections per image; the pipeline keeps at most 200,000
detections per image, which one image reached in one configuration without changing its mAP50. A pre-specified secondary
evaluation caps detections at 4,000 per image; it, the “all objects” evaluation and AP@[.5:.95] lead to the same
conclusions as the primary metric.
blocks.zh:

合成与现实的检测. 基本衡量尺度对每个图像的检测没有上限;管道最多保持20万

blocks.en:
Training. YOLOv10s and YOLOv10m were trained for 60 epochs at 1024 and 2048 px, with batches of eight and three images
(effective batch 64 and 63). At 2048 px, the CUDA allocator reported failed allocations in every epoch, which were absorbed by
retrying or by a per-image fallback of the label assignment that computes the same assignment; batch size and results are
unaffected. At 3072 px, training did not fit even with a batch of two, because of the object density. On calib, YOLOv10m at
2048 px stayed about 1.6 points below YOLOv10s over the whole late phase of training, whereas on DOTA-val it is ahead; the cause
remains open; possible explanations include batch normalisation with a batch of three, overfitting and the small calibration
split (141 images), which we did not test. YOLOv11s and YOLOv12s were added later under a dated addendum with unchanged hypotheses and
rules; YOLOv11s was trained at 1024 and 2048 px, whereas YOLOv12s did not fit at 2048 px even with a batch of two, so its
largest trainable pass is 1024 px and the questions that require 2048 px count as not confirmed for it.

blocks.en:
FCOS. FCOS (torchvision implementation, ResNet-50-FPN, COCO weights) was added last, under a further dated addendum with
unchanged hypotheses and rules, and as a single model it is judged without correction. Its recipe was fixed in advance and is
simpler than the Ultralytics recipe of the YOLO detectors: horizontal flips only, whereas the YOLO runs used mosaic, random
scaling by up to 50 % and translation. FCOS was trained at 1024 and 2048 px; at 2048 px with a batch of one image and
gradient accumulation to the same effective batch, which the pre-specified minimum batch of two does not forbid here because
FCOS uses group normalisation in its head and frozen batch normalisation in its backbone. Every FCOS configuration uses the
detector’s own score p ⋅ centerness \sqrt{p\cdot\text{centerness}} . Two observations are specific to FCOS. First, its best inference size
on calib was 2560 px for the 2048 px weights (the YOLO detectors preferred their training size), plausibly because its
recipe lacks scale augmentation; the pre-specified comparison against this best single pass is reported in the main text.
Second, the search of the refined grid selected the pre-specified cell factor for FCOS at both sizes, so its refined-grid rows
equal the pre-specified ones.

blocks.en:
Why SCAHI does not exceed box fusion for FCOS. Table 12 collects post-hoc diagnostics. Capping both
fusions at the same 200,000 detections per image leaves Q2 unchanged, so the uncapped output of box fusion is not the cause
(a). FCOS yields almost twice as many candidate predictions per object as the YOLO detectors (b), so a lack of redundant
evidence is not the cause either. With the coarse grid retained on calib, SCAHI recalls about 30 points fewer crowded objects
than box fusion, while isolated objects are recalled almost equally well (c): the over-merging analysed on VisDrone. Crowded
objects are only about 7 % of the objects on DOTA-val, which plausibly explains why selecting the cell factor by mAP50 on calib
did not favour a finer grid. Finally, the comparison is sensitive to the pipeline limit (d). The limit caps single very dense
images; without it, a few images contribute millions of low-scoring detections that rank above true positives of other images
and lower the dataset-wide precision. SCAHI then falls behind box fusion at 1024 px, and the gain of Q3 shrinks from 5.6 to
4.1 mAP50. The verdicts stay as computed under the pre-specified limit.

blocks.en:
SCAHI as a replacement for SAHI’s merge (Q4). For YOLOv10s/m, this comparison uses exactly the passes of the frozen SAHI
configuration (1024 px weights, SAHI’s 640 px slices and its standard full-image pass at 640 px). The caches reproduce SAHI’s own inference
path, including the fused model, one slice per forward pass and Ultralytics’ resize and back-mapping; recomputing SAHI from
them gives its frozen calib mAP50 exactly. SCAHI was tuned on calib as for all other rows. For YOLOv11s and YOLOv12s, which were added under a later addendum, SAHI was first
tuned on calib with the same procedure (both select an overlap of 0.2 and NMS), and SCAHI was then tuned on exactly these passes;
the two pairs were decided separately. Table 16 reports the results; the gain holds under every evaluation and for all
four detectors. Because YOLOv11s and YOLOv12s have a single dense head, SAHI and SCAHI see the same predictions there, which
isolates the merge step. By object size, SCAHI improves on SAHI in all bins above 8 px, most for
objects above 128 px (4.4 and 4.6 AP50), which SAHI’s slices cut into fragments. With the pre-specified setting, SCAHI lowers
the recall of crowded objects for every detector (e.g. 67 vs. 91 % for YOLOv10s, and by 17 and 19 points for YOLOv11s and
YOLOv12s); the refined grid restores it and lies above SAHI, as on the other configurations. With the fusion on the GPU, SAHI’s passes
followed by SCAHI take 147 and 219 ms per image for YOLOv10s and YOLOv10m, and SAHI itself 195 and 268 ms in the same run.
The difference in the passes (about 45 ms) is overhead of the SAHI library on the CPU, mainly image loading and per-detection
Python objects; it is not a property of SCAHI. SCAHI’s merge takes about 12 ms on the GPU, SAHI’s merge 14–16 ms on the CPU.

blocks.en:
The ablation was run after the main results, from the existing detections, on VisDrone val and on DOTA-val (the latter after
its single held-out evaluation); it never enters a verdict. All variants use the same passes (single pass at 2048 px plus
tiles) and the same parameter selection on calib. Figures 26 and 27 show all variants per detector,
including a sweep of the cell factor of the peak grid. On VisDrone, accuracy rises almost monotonically with the cell factor;
on DOTA it peaks around a cell factor of 9, while the recall of crowded objects keeps rising.

Why the normalisation has no effect. We measured the coverage C C at every fused position. With the coverage-aware
tapers and two levels of passes that each cover the whole image, C = 2 C=2 at every position on both datasets, so dividing by C C only rescales all scores. Without the taper, C C varies between 2 and 10 (mean about 3.4), and accuracy drops. That a pass
which covers a position but predicts nothing counts against an object follows from the summation over passes, not from the
division; the division would matter only for passes that cover part of the image, which our configurations do not contain.

blocks.en: 15 Societal impact
blocks.zh: 15 社会影响

blocks.en:
Object detection in aerial and UAV imagery supports beneficial applications such as search and rescue, disaster response,
traffic monitoring and infrastructure inspection. However, improving the detection and localisation of people and vehicles may
also facilitate intrusive surveillance and unauthorized monitoring. Although object detection does not establish individual
identities, its outputs could be combined with tracking or identification systems to infer sensitive information about
individuals and their movements. Our work does not identify individuals: it predicts class labels and boxes, and we used only
established public benchmarks (VisDrone, DOTA) as released by their creators, without collecting new data. Detection errors and
limited generalisation across environments may introduce additional risks in real-world use, and our results on public
benchmarks should not be read as evidence of suitability for high-stakes surveillance or automated decision-making. Responsible
deployment therefore requires appropriate privacy safeguards, data minimization, legal authorization and human oversight.
Finally, tiled inference multiplies the computation per image; where a single pass at a higher resolution suffices, as on
VisDrone in our experiments, it is also the more economical choice.
blocks.zh:
空中和无人驾驶航空器图像中的物体探测支持诸如搜索和救援、救灾等有益应用,
交通监测和基础设施检查。 然而,改善人员和车辆的检测和定位可能
还协助进行侵入性监视和未经授权的监测。 虽然物体检测不能确定个人
身份、其产出可与跟踪或识别系统相结合,以推断关于
个人及其运动。 我们的工作不识别个人:它预测阶级标签和盒子,我们只使用
建立了由创作者发布的公共基准(VisDrone, DOTA),而不收集新数据。 检测错误和
对环境的有限普遍化可能会给现实世界的利用带来更多的风险,而我们对公众的结果
不应将基准视为适合高额监测或自动决策的证据。 负责
因此,部署需要适当的隐私保障、尽量减少数据、法律授权和人员监督。
最后,推论将每个图像的计算乘以乘法;如果高分辨率的一次通过就够了,例如:
在我们的实验中,VisDrone也是更经济的选择。
